title: The Unix clock runs out of room in a signed 32-bit integer on January 19, 2038
assumption: A timestamp stored as 'seconds since the Unix epoch' can represent any date you throw at it.

input.display: 2**31 - 1 seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z == 2038-01-19T03:14:07Z; one more second overflows a signed 32-bit integer
input.description: Any system storing Unix time in a 32-bit signed integer column or struct field: older database schemas, C structs, embedded firmware, some binary file formats.

what_goes_wrong: A timestamp stored as a signed 32-bit seconds-since-epoch field wraps to a large negative number (around 1901) the instant it passes 2038-01-19T03:14:07Z, making a future date look like it's over a century in the past.
why: 2**31 - 1 (2,147,483,647) is the largest value a signed 32-bit integer can hold, and it corresponds to exactly 2038-01-19T03:14:07 UTC when interpreted as seconds since the Unix epoch. The next second would need to store 2**31, which a signed 32-bit integer cannot represent; it wraps around to -2**31, which as a Unix timestamp is in December 1901. Modern Python and JavaScript date objects aren't limited this way (Python's int is arbitrary precision and JS Date uses a 64-bit float of milliseconds), but anything that stores or transmits time as a literal signed 32-bit integer -- which includes plenty of still-running C code, old filesystems, and database columns -- is exposed exactly like a 2-digit-year Y2K bug, just 38 years later.

repros.code:
from datetime import datetime, timezone, timedelta

max_int32_seconds = 2**31 - 1
boundary = datetime(1970, 1, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc) + timedelta(seconds=max_int32_seconds)
print("last representable instant in signed 32-bit Unix time:", boundary)

# Simulate the wraparound a 32-bit signed integer would actually do.
def wrap_int32(n):
    n &= 0xFFFFFFFF
    return n - 0x100000000 if n >= 0x80000000 else n

print("next second, wrapped to signed 32-bit:", wrap_int32(max_int32_seconds + 1))
repros.expected_output:
last representable instant in signed 32-bit Unix time: 2038-01-19 03:14:07+00:00
next second, wrapped to signed 32-bit: -2147483648

boundary instant: 2038-01-19T03:14:07.000Z
next second, wrapped to signed 32-bit: -2147483648

fix: Never store a timestamp in a signed 32-bit field for anything that must outlive 2038; use a 64-bit integer (or your language's native arbitrary-precision/64-bit date type) for any seconds-since-epoch storage, and audit older schemas and binary formats specifically for this.
